Figure 1:What the farm delivers.(a)The same frame of a simulator rollout and of our H3 rendering for each of the five tasks; the
rendering is photographic and keeps the simulated arm pose, objects, and contacts (insets enlarge the dashed regions).(b)From a request and one calibration episode, the agent builds the task in simulation, and the video
model renders each rollout in the original scene or in a new scene described by text.(c)Real-robot successes of policies trained only on farm data or on the same number of teleoperated
episodes, in the original scene and under unseen appearance.(d)Mean costs over the five tasks (Section6.2).

Figure 2:Overview ofDataFarm.(1)A request and one calibration episode of the scene are the only inputs.(2)A coding agent rebuilds the task in simulation and writes an expert against a judge it cannot see; the simulator then runs the expert from many initial states and fixes the actions, object states, and contacts.(3)A video model conditioned on real frames renders every rollout in the scene’s appearance, and a new appearance is a text change.(4)An independent reviewer compares each render with its simulated state, and only admitted episodes enter the dataset.Bottom:the farm pays once per task rather than for every episode, and its data matches teleoperated data on the real robot. Shown on the pull-drawer task; the cost plot is schematic.

Figure 3:TheDataFarmpipeline, followed on one drawer episode.The agent builds five
intermediate representations: the groundingGG, whose quantities are each labelled by how they are known;
the task contractTTand the expertCC, written against a hidden judgeJJ; the simulated episodesEE; the
rendered observationsOO; and the admission recordqq. Each representation is checked by a component other
than its producer (seals), and a rejection returns to the stage that caused it (dashed), as for the render here
that shows an arm absent fromEE. The capability layer𝒦\mathcal{K}is shared by all tasks; everything above
it is written for this task.

Figure 4:Real-robot results.(a)Successes ofπ0.5\pi_{0.5}policies trained
on 100 episodes from each source, in 20 trials per task and condition (Total: out of 100), in the original
scene (left) and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light (right).(b)Unseen-scene trials in which the policy trained on teleoperated data fails (top) and the policy
trained only on farm data succeeds (bottom).

Figure 7:Real, simulated, and farm episodesat the same task phase (head view).
Sim + DR adds domain-randomized textures and lighting to the simulator frame, and ours renders the simulator
frame (renderer in the corner). Real and simulated frames come from different episodes, so object placements
differ.

Figure 8:Following the simulation in every view.The same simulated frame rendered by calling the video model
directly, with all cameras on one canvas or with each camera separately, and by the farm’s renderer. Each
cell shows the head view (top) and the left and right wrist views (bottom). Red boxes mark the views that
contradict the simulator or the other views of the same frame; the notes describe the contradiction.

Figure 9:Appearance that the simulator does not model.Crops of a simulator frame
(top) and of the farm episode rendered from that frame (middle), with the same object in a real recording at
the same task phase (bottom; not the same frame). The simulator draws the scale’s display as a flat
texture, the drum as a red cylinder, and the towel as smooth particle cloth; the farm episode shows a lit
display with the simulated reading, a lacquered drum with brass tacks, and the weave of the real towel.
